articles.title: Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese spark Kelsey Mitchell’s ‘You can’t gatekeep’ warning over WNBA’s changing landscape
articles.summary: Kelsey Mitchell has made her view on Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese clear: the WNBA should welcome young stars instead of trying to keep them out.
articles.body: Kelsey Mitchell has made her view on Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese clear: the WNBA should welcome young stars instead of trying to keep them out. The Indiana Fever veteran said Clark and Reese have helped open new doors for women’s basketball and brought more attention to the league. Mitchell, who has played alongside Clark since the Fever drafted her in 2024, spoke about the pair in her recent SLAM cover story. Her comments come as the WNBA continues to see strong interest around its biggest young names, with Clark and Reese playing a major part in that wider conversation.Kelsey Mitchell explains Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese impactClark and Reese entered the WNBA in 2024 after being two of the biggest names in college basketball. Their rivalry from college followed them into the league, and games involving the two quickly became major draws.The numbers from that season showed just how much interest the WNBA was getting. According to the WNBA, the league recorded its highest total attendance in 22 years in 2024, with 2,353,735 fans attending games. Total attendance was up 48% from the previous season, while the league recorded 154 sellouts.Mitchell sees that growth as something the league should embrace. Rather than treating new stars as a threat to established players, she believes their arrival can create more opportunities for everyone involved in women’s basketball.“You can’t gatekeep,” Mitchell said. “It would only pigeonhole our game. When Angel Reese and CC came in … it opened up so many doors for us.”The comments were made in Mitchell’s interview with SLAM, where she discussed the changing WNBA and the effect of a new group of young players. SLAM also shared a clip of Mitchell discussing her views on the league’s growth.Caitlin Clark, Kelsey Mitchell have built Fever partnershipMitchell has had a close view of Clark’s WNBA career from the beginning. The two have been teammates in Indiana since Clark arrived as the No. 1 pick in the 2024 WNBA Draft. By 2026, both had become All-Stars, with Mitchell selected as a 2026 All-Star starter alongside Clark.Their partnership has also become an important part of the Fever’s offense. In August 2026, the pair both scored more than 20 points in several games, while Mitchell continued to set new marks during a strong individual season. The Fever’s own coverage has regularly highlighted the two guards working together on the court.At the same time, Clark and Reese remain linked through the rivalry that began before they entered the WNBA. Reese now plays for the Atlanta Dream, while Clark continues to lead the Fever alongside Mitchell. The league has continued to feature their matchups as part of its growing rivalries.For Mitchell, the bigger point is just the attention around players such as Clark and Reese can help bring more people to women’s basketball. Her message is not about choosing one generation over another. She is arguing that the WNBA can make room for new stars while still respecting the players who helped build the league.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Asian Games 2026: Ankush Panghal punches India’s first boxing medal with 5-0 quarterfinal win
articles.summary: Reigning Commonwealth Games champion Ankush Panghal delivered a commanding performance on Sunday to assure India of its first boxing medal at the Asian
articles.body: Reigning Commonwealth Games champion Ankush Panghal delivered a commanding performance on Sunday to assure India of its first boxing medal at the Asian Games 2026, defeating Tajikistan's Nekruz Salimov by a unanimous 5-0 decision in the men's 80kg quarterfinals.Ankush controlled the contest for most of the three rounds, using his speed, sharp combinations and solid defence to establish a decisive advantage before holding off a late challenge from Salimov.Ankush dominates first two roundsThe Indian boxer came out aggressively and immediately put Salimov under pressure with a combination of right hooks and crisp 1-2 punches. Ankush won the opening round unanimously, with all five judges scoring it in his favour. He continued to dictate the pace in the second round, showcasing his movement and counter-punching ability while making it difficult for Salimov to land clean shots.His powerful left hook proved particularly effective as he secured another 5-0 verdict in the second round, leaving the Tajik boxer needing a major turnaround in the final three minutes.Salimov fights back, but Ankush holds firmWith his tournament on the line, Salimov came out with greater urgency in the third round and looked to land heavier punches in search of a knockdown. The Tajik boxer managed to connect with a few shots and took the final round 4-1 on the judges' scorecards. However, Ankush had already built a comfortable lead and remained composed until the final bell.Four judges scored the bout 29-28 in Ankush's favour, while the fifth judge awarded him a 30-27 victory, completing a convincing 5-0 win. The quarterfinal victory guarantees Ankush at least a bronze medal, while the CWG champion will now turn his attention to the semifinals as he bids to go one step further.Kurash campaign ends for Indian athletesIndia's campaign in kurash, meanwhile, suffered a series of setbacks on Sunday. Vishal was knocked out in the men's +90kg quarterfinals after losing 5-0 to Thailand's Kunathip Yea-On.In the women's -57kg category, Sangita Balhara suffered a 10-0 defeat against the Philippines' Charmea Quelino in the Round of 32. Bharti was eliminated in the Round of 16 after losing to Iran's Tahereh Azarpeivand, while Yash Kumar Chauhan also exited the men's +90kg competition following a 10-0 defeat to Tajikistan's Shakarmamad Mirmamadov.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Asian Games: PV Sindhu, Unnati Hooda exits cap disappointing badminton campaign as India return with just one medal
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India’s badminton campaign at the Asian Games 2026 ended on Sunday with a disappointing return of just one medal, as PV Sindhu and Unnati Hooda
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India’s badminton campaign at the Asian Games 2026 ended on Sunday with a disappointing return of just one medal, as PV Sindhu and Unnati Hooda bowed out in the women’s singles quarterfinals after spirited efforts against formidable opponents.Two-time Olympic medallist Sindhu went down 21-11, 18-21, 10-21 to Tokyo Olympic champion Chen Yu Fei of China, while 19-year-old Hooda pushed three-time world champion Akane Yamaguchi of Japan before losing 16-21, 21-14, 17-21.The exits meant India failed to win a medal in any of the individual badminton events, with the men’s team bronze remaining the country’s only podium finish at Aichi-Nagoya. The contrast with the previous edition in Hangzhou was stark: India had won three medals there, including men’s team silver, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty’s doubles gold, and HS Prannoy’s singles bronze.Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | ScheduleSindhu fades after strong start against ChenSindhu, who had already played twice on Saturday, was competing for the third time in less than 24 hours. She started strongly against Chen, taking control of the opening game with sharp movement and aggressive shot-making to win it 21-11.The Indian also stayed in contention through much of the second game, which was closely fought and featured long rallies. The pair were level at 16-16 before Chen edged ahead to take the game 21-18 and force a decider.Chen seized control in the third, opening up an early lead and taking an 11-7 advantage at the interval. Sindhu managed only three more points after the break as the Chinese won 10 of the next 11 points to close out the match.Sindhu had entered the quarterfinal with a 7-9 head-to-head record against Chen, whom she had beaten on the way to winning the Japan Open Super 750 title in July. But the Indian could not repeat that result after a demanding schedule over the previous day.Hooda fights back but Yamaguchi holds onHooda also showed resilience in her quarterfinal against world No. 3 Yamaguchi, recovering from a one-sided opening game to take the second and force a decider.The Japanese controlled the early exchanges in the first game, using a range of strokes to build a sizeable lead and eventually take it 21-16. Hooda responded with a strong attacking display in the second, pulling level at 7-7 and then moving ahead as Yamaguchi began making errors. The Indian won eight successive points to claim the game 21-14.The decider remained tight, with the players level at 5-5 before Yamaguchi established a lead. Hooda continued to extend rallies and challenge the Japanese, but Yamaguchi held her advantage and closed out the match 21-17.Doubles pairs also fall in quarterfinalsIndia’s remaining doubles hopes had ended earlier on Sunday. Women’s pair Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand, fresh from winning a maiden World Championships bronze last month, lost 18-21, 9-21 to Malaysia’s world No. 5 combination of Pearly Tan and Thinaah Muralitharan.In mixed doubles, Dhruv Kapila and Tanisha Crasto came close to upsetting the world No. 1 Chinese pair of Feng Yan Zhe and Huang Dongping, but eventually lost 14-21, 21-18, 18-21.Heavy schedule adds to players’ workloadThe demanding schedule was another talking point, with Sindhu, Hooda and Ayush Shetty among the players required to contest two matches within a few hours on Saturday. Sindhu’s quarterfinal against Chen was her third match in less than 24 hours, while Hooda also faced a taxing turnaround before her last-eight clash.Despite the effort and resilience shown by India’s leading shuttlers, the campaign ended well short of the three-medal return from Hangzhou. With only the men’s team bronze to show from Aichi-Nagoya, India’s badminton contingent leaves the Games without an individual-event medal.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: A's Have One More Game to Play Spoiler Against Houston
articles.summary: In addition to playing spoiler on Sunday, the A's will have an achievement of their own worth chasing.
articles.body:
The Athletics have been out of the hunt for October for weeks and will finish the season with the best odds of landing the No. 1 pick in the 2027 MLB Draft at 19.1%. That doesn't mean that they don't have something to play for on Sunday afternoon against the Houston Astros in the regular season finale.

With one game left, the Astros and Texas Rangers are tied atop the division with each team holding an 80-81 record. The Astros hold the tiebreaker over Texas, so a tie does the Rangers no good. That means Texas needs an A's win in order to have a shot at playing in October. They also need to win their own game to make that quest a reality.

A Houston win means they're in. A Texas loss eliminates the Rangers.

The A's will be going with all hands on deck on the mound. Seth Johnson will be serving as the team's opener, but Mark Kotsay has been adamant for weeks that his team wants to play spoiler. Sunday presents a key opportunity to end someone's season. It wouldn't be surprising to see the team empty out the bullpen chasing a win if one is within reach.

That's why Yunior Tur tossing the final 2 ⅓ innings and throwing 46 pitches on Saturday night could end up being a key factor on Sunday, as most of the primary relief options will have had a day off heading in, likely making them available for the final game.

The other thing the A's will be playing for is a bit of pride. Going into the series, they had a winning record against every team in the AL West. With Houston winning two of the first three games of this series, the Astros have evened up the season record at 6-6. A win on Sunday for the A's would put them back ahead 7-6 on the year.

The A's also held a 7-6 record against the Seattle Mariners and Rangers, and went 8-5 against the Angels . Despite holding a 64-97 record, holding a winning record against each team in the division would be one bright spot in an otherwise forgettable year.

Given the number of injuries the A's have faced this season and the lack of pitching needed to compete for much of the year, holding a winning record against each team in the division would be a huge confidence boost for the club going into next season when they will presumably be a bit healthier and have a little more pitching depth.

articles.title: USC has seen enough and it’s time to move on from Lincoln Riley
articles.summary: As Lincoln Riley walked off the field at the Coliseum on Saturday night after a 41-27 loss to Oregon, the result seemed much larger than the team’s first los...
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES — As Lincoln Riley walked off the field at the Coliseum on Saturday night after a 41-27 loss to Oregon , the result seemed much larger than the team's first loss of the season.

USC might be 4-1, but Trojans fans have seen this Riley production before, and they've lost interest in sticking around for the inevitable disappointing ending. The early victories create optimism. The first major disappointment comes with assurances that everything the team wants remains possible. Then the losses accumulate, and another season that began with playoff aspirations ends with everyone being asked to get excited about next year.

In 2025, USC started 4-0 before going 5-4 the rest of the season, culminating in a collapse against TCU in the Alamo Bowl. In 2024, USC started 3-1 before going 3-5 to finish the regular season. In 2023, USC started 6-0 before going 1-5 to finish the regular season.

Riley's high-water mark at USC remains his first season in 2022, and even that year offered a preview of what was coming. The Trojans lost to Utah in the Pac-12 championship game with the program's first College Football Playoff berth on the line, then blew a 15-point lead to Tulane in the final four minutes of the Cotton Bowl.

That history is why Saturday's fourth-quarter collapse felt so familiar. In his fifth season, Riley is still explaining why USC couldn't finish a game that could have changed how people view his program. At some point, those explanations become the strongest argument for finding someone else to lead it.

Riley is unlikely to be fired because of the Oregon loss, but USC should begin moving toward a future without him. There is too much evidence now to keep treating these performances as isolated disappointments on the way to something better.

The Trojans tied the game at 27 with 12:41 remaining when Jayden Maiava found Tanook Hines for an 11-yard touchdown. A sold-out crowd of 75,500 had every reason to believe this could finally be the night USC finished the job. The energy was there. The opportunity was there. Even Riley acknowledged afterward that the Coliseum had delivered everything his team could have wanted.

"That moment was probably the most rowdy I've heard our crowd since I've been here," Riley said. "It was a hell of an atmosphere in the Coliseum. We had all the momentum in the world."

Then USC did what it has done too often under Riley. It gave the opportunity away.

With Oregon facing third-and-15 from its own 40, an incomplete pass should have put the Trojans in position to get the ball back. Instead, a roughing-the-passer penalty against Jide Abasiri extended the possession. Oregon eventually scored on Dylan Raiola 's 29-yard touchdown pass to Dakorien Moore , and USC spent the rest of the night chasing a game it never caught.

The Trojans turned the ball over on downs at their own 49 on the next possession. Oregon then took 5:12 off the clock before Jordon Davison 's 2-yard touchdown run made it 41-27 with 2:03 remaining. After tying the score, USC allowed 14 unanswered points and never scored again.

The penalty mattered, but reducing this loss to one player's mistake would let the head coach off far too easily. USC surrendered 504 yards, failed to record a sack or force a turnover, and allowed Oregon to convert both of its fourth-down attempts. Riley's offense finished 2 for 11 on third down. There was plenty of responsibility to spread around.

Oregon also had to replace starting quarterback Dante Moore after USC linebacker Desman Stephens blasted him as he gave himself up and slid for a first down. Stephens was ejected for targeting but Riley allowed him to stay on USC's sideline even after celebrating the vicious cheap hit. Raiola came off the bench and completed 19 of 25 passes for 289 yards and two touchdowns. USC couldn't take control against a team forced to make that adjustment on the road, in front of the loudest crowd Riley could remember during his tenure.

The Ducks were prepared to respond to adversity. USC was left explaining its response to opportunity.

"We had exactly what we wanted," Riley said. "But against good teams, if you give them opportunities to stay in the game or give them that fresh set of downs, it's tough to beat good teams that way."

He is right. He has also been here long enough for USC to expect a team that understands that before the postgame press conference. Discipline, tackling, communication and execution on critical downs are the head coach's responsibility. When those shortcomings keep deciding the biggest games, going back to work cannot be the entire answer.

The most revealing part of Riley's press conference came when he was asked about the evolution of his defense.

"I don't make big picture statements after a game," he said. "We just finished the game an hour ago."

He continued: "This is not about any of the games before. It's not about any of the games coming up. That's just a fantasy world. That's not what we live in."

Riley can ask his players to focus on the next practice and the next opponent. That is understandable. But USC cannot evaluate its head coach by pretending every Saturday exists independently of everything that came before it. The previous games are his record. The repeated collapses are his history. Looking at them together is how a university determines whether its football program is headed in the right direction.

The issues at USC run deeper than Riley, and replacing him won't automatically solve them. The university has to examine why it keeps finding itself here. But acknowledging institutional problems doesn't require keeping a coach who has failed to provide a convincing reason to believe the results will change.

Riley can still have success somewhere else. USC has seen that before. Pete Carroll won a Super Bowl after leaving. Ed Orgeron won a national championship at LSU . Lane Kiffin and Steve Sarkisian rebuilt their careers after humiliating exits. A coach's departure from USC doesn't have to be the end of his story, and the school doesn't have to keep waiting for his redemption to happen here.

On Saturday, Riley lost more than a game. He lost the trust of fans who had shown up ready to believe again, along with several boosters who hadn't texted me about the state of the program since Clay Helton was at the helm. Their frustration carried the exhaustion of people who have had this conversation too many times.

No one can know after five games exactly where this season will end. USC still has an opportunity to respond. But the burden should be on Riley to produce something different, not on everyone else to explain why they no longer expect it.

The Coliseum showed Saturday that the appetite for USC football is still there. Those fans want meaningful games, championship expectations and a reason to believe their program can meet the moment. They gave Riley another chance to show them that future against Oregon.

He gave them another reminder of the past. USC has waited long enough to turn the page.

articles.title: Marquez could benefit at any moment after Martin takes MotoGP injury gamble
articles.summary: MotoGP championship leader Jorge Martin has received a stark warning over his decision to opt against surgery. The Aprilia rider took the lead back from Marc...
articles.body:
MotoGP championship leader Jorge Martin has received a stark warning over his decision to opt against surgery.

The Aprilia rider took the lead back from Marc Marquez in Austria, a week on from arm pump taking him out of the battle in Misano.

Ahead of his impressive sprint victory and second place in the Grand Prix at the Red Bull Ring, Martin said he would decide on surgery the Monday after the weekend concluded.

However, with such a strong showing, he then admitted he didn't feel it was necessary, and that rest was the best option for his ailment.

Yet his vastly experienced agent, Carlo Pernat, has suggested the call could backfire at any moment.

Pernat has worked with a number of the sport's greats, and is more than familiar with how arm pump can strike at any moment.

Martin warned arm pump could occur without warning

Speaking to MotoSan, he said: "Martin has decided against surgery, and he probably made the right choice because the championship is very important to him.

"But he should be careful, because this compartment syndrome can strike suddenly, almost without warning, and the arm can become unusable.

"Regarding his choice, I would say that 50% of the decision is correct and 50% is incorrect. We'll see. I hope it was the right one…"

"It can strike suddenly, almost without warning, and the arm can become unusable."

Martin may have missed key window for operation

Arm pump is an issue almost every rider has experienced and is the colloquial term for chronic exertional compartment syndrome.

The issue is common in all forms of motorcycle racing and is alleviated by an insertion into the arm and removal of fascia.

Martin may have missed a key window for surgery , with a two-week break between Austria and Japan, followed by Indonesia a week later.

For Pernat, he now has only two title rivals, Marquez and Aprilia teammate Marco Bezzecchi.

Pernat names three riders in MotoGP title fight

He added: "This World Championship is being fought between three riders: Marquez, Martin, and Bezzecchi.

"It's a shame for Ai Ogura, who crashed a couple of times before his injury, but he showed what he's made of. And it's also a shame for Pedro [Acosta] , who crashed in the sprint when he could have accumulated another 12 points and closed the gap even further.

"Perhaps the World Championship wouldn't really have been decided, but it would have made everything even more interesting. It's truly a great world championship."

articles.title: Ayden Fernandez, strong defense power Reagan past Brandeis for first victory
articles.summary: The two-way athlete took on a bigger role as a running back to lead the Rattlers' offense as Reagan opened District 28-6A with a win over the Broncos.
articles.body:
Ayden Fernandez splits his time on both sides of the ball for Reagan, but the Rattlers turned to him to take on a bigger role on offense Saturday.

The two-way athlete rushed for 164 yards and two scores in leading Reagan to a 35-20 win over the Brandeis Broncos in a District 28-6A game at Farris Stadium.

Behind Fernandez's big rushing night and a defense which produced two interceptions returns for scores, Reagan (1-3, 1-0) picked up its first win of the season after losing its first three games. Most importantly, the Rattlers opened district play on the right note against Brandeis (2-2, 0-1), preserving a 7-0 record in the all-time series between the two teams.

Fernandez, a senior who also plays linebacker, said the improved Reagan rushing attack was the result of the work the offensive line has put in at practice.

"Our offensive line, these past two weeks we've been working on downhill run, downhill run, and that's what we did, downhill run," Fernandez said. "They can't stop it."

Reagan coach Preston Meyer said Fernandez is going to be seeing more time in the offensive backfield for the remainder of the season.

"If you're going to win football games, you got to be able to run the ball," Meyer said. "Ayden (Fernandez) had been playing some running back, but we decided let's give him a bigger role on the offensive side of the football. He can still play a little defense, but he's going to be our primary running back moving forward."

While Brandeis senior quarterback Wynter Smith rushed for 110 yards and one score, Reagan's defense limited the dual threat signal caller to 8-of-26 passing. Jayden Horace and Steven Robinson each returned interceptions for touchdowns for the Rattlers, and defensive end Emiliano Berlin sacked Smith twice.

"Well, we knew going into it, their quarterback would run around and make a lot of plays with his feet and with his arm," Meyer said. "But going into it, we knew if we could slow him down and give him trouble then we would be successful defensively. We knew you can't just go crazy, trying to bring pressure and rush him because he'll split you, and so we just wanted to keep the eyes on the quarterback, play some zone, underneath zone coverage. That way when he did try to escape, we had eyes on him ready to go, try to get him on the ground."

Reagan scored its first touchdown before its offensive unit got on the field, as Robinson picked off a Smith pass on the game's first possession, returning it 65 yards for the score with 8:29 left in the first quarter.

The Rattlers extended their lead to 14-0 late in the first quarter, as Fernandez scored his first touchdown on a 1-yarder, with sophomore Jayson Sinclair setting up Fernandez's score with a 32-yard scamper to the Brandeis 1-yard line.

Brandeis scored on two consecutive drives in the second quarter to tie the game at 14, first on a 26-yard scoring run from Smith, then on a 28-yard touchdown pass down the middle from Smith to sophomore Jacob De La O.

Reagan regained the lead on the ensuing possession. Quarterback Jace Huesser utilized the play-action fake to connect with tight end Russell Reed for a 72-yard touchdown catch with 3:27 remaining in the first half, giving the Rattlers a 21-14 halftime advantage.

Reagan struck quickly in the second half as Fernandez scored on a 43-yard run on the fourth play to put the Rattlers up by two touchdowns just over a minute into the third quarter.

Fernandez said his second touchdown run further boosted the energy level of his teammates.

"It was definitely energy once I scored," Fernandez said. "I came back on the sideline, everyone's up, it feels good. It 100 percent set the tone (for the rest of the game). After that we were firing, offense, special teams, defense and when a team is firing on all three phases, you can't beat them."

Brandeis chipped into the Reagan lead as Zach Cantu booted field goals of 41 and 49 yards on consecutive possessions to put the Broncos within 28-20 with 15 seconds left in the third quarter.

Reagan continued to grind it out on the ground in the second half, as Fernandez and Sinclair each carried the ball on a long drive that put the Rattlers at the Brandeis 11 in the fourth quarter. The drive set up a field goal attempt, but Brandeis blocked it to keep the game within one score.

But the momentum from the blocked field goal attempt would be short lived for the Broncos, as Reagan brought the pressure on Smith, whose pass was picked off by Horace for a 45-yard touchdown, sealing the win for the Rattlers with 6:13 left in the game.

articles.title: Former 76ers GM gives fans reason to be happy even when LeBron James, Joel Embiid ‘are out’
articles.summary: Former Sixers general manager Billy King explains that fans have something to look forward to even when their new superstar core misses time. The Philadelphi...
articles.body:
Former Sixers general manager Billy King explains that fans have something to look forward to even when their new superstar core misses time.

The Philadelphia 76ers have put together an incredible core. With Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey staying on the roster, the franchise has managed to add Jaylen Brown and LeBron James .

With a starting five that includes these four names, an NBA championship has become the expectation. However, there have been concerns about their ability to play many games together.

And now a former franchise executive has weighed in on the matter, discussing how fans won't be left high and dry even if the superstars can't play.

Billy King claims the Sixers' younger stars and bench can win games without Joel Embiid and LeBron James

The Philadelphia 76ers roster outside of the four stars and rookie sensation VJ Edgecombe has some interesting names. The team has added role players like Dean Wade , Kentavious Caldwell-Pope , and Anfernee Simons , among others.

That is not bad depth at all. They have physicality, shooting, and championship experience. Former franchise GM Billy King pointed this out when talking about the team recently.

"What they've done, is they've added some good bench pieces, which they never had here" King said about the Sixers. "The starting guys have been great but they didn't have enough depth.

"But they've added some good, young bench players. So when those guys are out… Say Joel and LeBron are out, you've still got a squad with Jaylen, VJ, Maxey, and the bench pieces they have added.

"So I think that team will have a chance to really continue to win when those guys are out."

King did say that the superstars would have to ultimately be healthy if the Sixers are to win. But his point about the bench situation is valid. If the 76ers have any two of their Big 4 on the court with the rest of the roster, they will still be in good shape against anyone.

Cam Skattebo revealed the physical impact of playing football on his shoulder, and fans are worried the New York Giants ' future may have just gone from bad to worse.

The Giants have already lost Jaxson Dart to a season-ending knee surgery, forcing John Harbaugh to rely on Jameis Winston as their starting quarterback for the rest of the year.

Cam Skattebo's shoulder has fans concerned about his future

During a livestream, New York Giants RB Cam Skattebo revealed the impact years of playing football have had on his shoulder.

He moved his sweatshirt to show a massive bump on his shoulder joint that is so sharp that he can use it to scratch his chin.

"Chat, I've got a twin right here. I scratch my chin with this."

Understandably, fans were very concerned about the way Skattebo's shoulder looks, with many suggesting that his career could be cut short by this.

One fan wrote, "AC separation. I have one too. From snowboarding….. I'm done snowboarding."

Another fan added, "That's not supposed to do that!"

A third fan shared his concern, noting, "Does bro have a broken collarbone and just acting like it's no big deal? Holy c***."

"He gonna be 35 begging to be shut down," wrote a fourth fan detailing the impact this injury could have had on his long-term career.

A fifth fan noted, "He won't last," admitting that Skattebo's injury could cut his career short.

And lastly, one fan pointed out how his injury serves as a contrast to another great NFL RB, saying, "It took Keenan Allen almost ten years in the league to grow his."

Clearly, Skattebo has suffered many shoulder injuries during his career, and his injuries have taken a huge toll on his body.

It is possible that these injuries could have a significant impact on his career and possibly cut his career short.

articles.title: Asian Games 2026: What Indian medallists can earn in cash rewards, government jobs and state incentives
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India’s medal winners at the Asian Games 2026 could return home with more than a place on the podium.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India’s medal winners at the Asian Games 2026 could return home with more than a place on the podium. Along with national recognition, athletes who win gold, silver or bronze are eligible for cash awards under a central government scheme. They may also qualify for sports-quota jobs and additional incentives announced by their respective state governments.The central cash awards are laid out in the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports’ “Special Awards to Medal Winners in International Sports Events and their Coaches” scheme. The scheme, first introduced in 1986, has been revised over time, with the stated aim of rewarding sporting achievement, encouraging higher performance and inspiring young people to take up sports.For an individual Asian Games medal, the listed central award is Rs 30 lakh for gold, Rs 20 lakh for silver and Rs 10 lakh for bronze. These are the base figures: the amount for a team medal depends on the size of the team and the scheme’s rules for calculating and distributing awards.Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | ScheduleHow much does an individual medallist receive?Under the central scheme, Asian Games and Commonwealth Games medal awards are the same. Olympic medal awards are higher.CompetitionGoldSilverBronzeOlympic GamesRs 75 lakhRs 50 lakhRs 30 lakhAsian GamesRs 30 lakhRs 20 lakhRs 10 lakhCommonwealth GamesRs 30 lakhRs 20 lakhRs 10 lakhThe same corresponding award amounts apply to Para Games medal winners. The cash incentive is subject to the eligibility criteria and conditions prescribed by the government.That means an Indian athlete who wins an individual gold in Aichi-Nagoya could be eligible for a central award of Rs 30 lakh. A silver medallist’s listed award is Rs 20 lakh, while a bronze medallist’s is Rs 10 lakh.Team medals: the calculation changesFor team events, the scheme determines the award using the number of athletes in the team on the ground. The multiplier is applied to the corresponding individual-event award for the competition, medal and category.A team of two receives 1.5 times the corresponding award; a team of three or four receives twice the award; a team of five to 10 receives three times the award; and a team with more than 10 members receives five times the award. The resulting amount is shared equally among the team members, with a condition that no member receives less than 50% of the corresponding individual-event award.The scheme defines team events as competitions in which athletes compete collectively, and says incentives are awarded to all team members, including bench or reserve players, in accordance with the international standards applicable to each sport. It also provides that, in specified sports disciplines, each team member’s cash incentive is 75% of the incentive amount applicable to the corresponding individual event, based on the medal, level and participation category.These provisions mean that a team medal cannot simply be treated as the same flat award for every athlete. The final amount depends on the event’s classification, team strength and applicable scheme provisions.Multiple medals and the highest-award ruleThe scheme also addresses athletes who win more than one medal at an international event. As a general rule, a sportsperson who wins multiple medals in individual or team categories is eligible for the cash incentive only for the highest-ranking medal won at that event.There is an important exception for the Olympic Games, Paralympic Games, Asian Games and Para-Asian Games: athletes who win multiple medals in individual or team categories may be eligible for the cash incentive for each medal, subject to the scheme’s terms and conditions.For an Asian Games athlete who wins more than one medal, therefore, the central award may be calculated medal by medal rather than being limited to the single highest finish. The precise amount still depends on whether the medals were won individually or as part of a team, and on the applicable team-event rules.The figures and provisions above are from the Department of Sports, Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports circular dated January 31, 2025, as provided in the scheme details.Can Asian Games medallists get government jobs?Cash awards are only one part of the potential support available to medal winners. Athletes who have represented India in recognised international competitions, including the Asian Games, may also be considered for recruitment under sports-quota provisions.At the central level, recruitment of meritorious sportspersons is governed by Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) instructions and related office memorandums. The central framework generally provides for appointment to Group C and erstwhile Group D posts, subject to eligibility, recruitment rules and the specific terms in force. It does not establish a general entitlement for every medal winner to receive a Group A or Group B post.A medal does not, by itself, mean that a job is automatically granted. Athletes must meet the relevant conditions, and appointments depend on the applicable recruitment process and rules. Serving government employees may also be covered by separate provisions, including certain out-of-turn promotion or incentive arrangements, where permitted.State incentives can add another layerThe amount an athlete may receive after the Games can vary further because state governments frame their own sports policies and service rules. Some states offer additional cash awards, employment opportunities or other incentives to athletes from their state who win medals at major international competitions.As a result, two Indian athletes who win the same medal at the Asian Games may be eligible for different overall benefits depending on their state’s policy and their individual circumstances. State incentives are not uniform across India, and any announced reward or job offer must be checked against the specific state’s policy, eligibility conditions and formal government orders.For athletes and families assessing what a medal could mean financially, the key distinction is between the central scheme’s published cash award and any separate state-level benefit. The central award schedule gives a clear starting point – Rs 30 lakh, Rs 20 lakh and Rs 10 lakh for individual Asian Games gold, silver and bronze – but the final package may depend on team-event calculations, multiple-medal provisions, state rules and eligibility for recruitment or other incentives.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: College Football Rankings Week 5: Possibly Our Craziest Top 25 Yet
articles.summary: We're not happy about the latest CFN Top 25 rankings, but for now, this is how we have to do them going into Week 5. We're sorry.
articles.body:
Before you go one step further with the Week 5 CFN Top 25, please understand one extremely important disclaimer: We don't like our rankings this week, either. There's a Grand Canyon-sized glitch happening at the moment, and there's just no way around it until next week, at least – Tulsa beat Oklahoma State 24-10 in Week 1 (and it wasn't some last-second Hail Mary thing). We've done our rankings the same way ever since we started in 1998 – always go by what happened on the field, regardless of school name, beliefs, or hype, and then, as the season goes on, there's a combination of Respect The Results along with our sane and rational judgment. So please, be kind, understand that we totally get it, and yes, there will be massive changes coming soon.

CFN Week 5 Top 25 Teams: It Has To Be This Way, For Now

Record: (3-1) Last Week Rank: 38 Week 4: Oregon 41, USC 27 Up Next: OPEN DATE And here's our problem. We want to rank Oregon because it really is one of the 25 best teams in college football – and, honestly, when it's humming, it probably belongs in the top five. We also want to give the Ducks credit for beating USC, but there's a problem with that, too – USC's wins were against San Jose State, Fresno State, Louisiana, and it struggled against a lousy Rutgers team that got whacked by UMass. Trade the USC name for, say, Purdue, with the same sort of resume and results, and the win wouldn't be that big of a deal. But to rank Oregon means we have to respect the 39-31 loss to a 3-1 Oklahoma State team that we also want to rank, so …

Record: (3-1) Last Week Rank: 37 Week 4: Oklahoma State 41, West Virginia 24 Up Next: OPEN DATE The win over West Virginia in Morgantown was fantastic. The Cowboys are up to speed, looking great over the last three weeks against the Mountaineers, Murray State, and, of course, Oregon. So to do this correctly – for now – we must rank the Cowboys ahead of the Ducks, which means we (seriously, we're holding our noses here) have to rank …

Record: (3-1) Last Week Rank: 36 Week 4: Arkansas 34, Tulsa 6 Up Next: North Texas Again, Tulsa stuffed this Cowboy team in Week 1 in a 24-10 win, and it was even more impressive than you might think. The Golden Hurricane were up 17-3 late in the third, forced four turnovers, and were only outgained by seven yards. So for now, Tulsa has to be ranked higher than Oklahoma State, which means – and hold on to your butts on this …

Record: (2-2) Last Week Rank: 75 Week 4: Arkansas 34, Tulsa 6 Up Next: at Texas A&M Before you holler at us, remember who the two Arkansas losses were against. Georgia, who might win the national title, and Utah, who might at least win the Big 12 Championship. Those two are destroying everyone, not just Arkansas, who just blew out Tulsa, making this the hardest piece of the puzzle to fit. And with that, the top 21 becomes a tad more normal.

Record: (4-0) Last Week Rank: 55 Week 4: Cincinnati 31, Kansas State 26 Up Next: at Arizona After screaming from the rooftops for the last six months that Kansas State was terrific, now we have to give the just-due credit to the team that beat the team we liked so much. Also, Washington State put up a fight against Washington and Arizona, and got whacked by the Bearcats by 27.

Record: (4-0) Last Week Rank: 43 Week 4: Nebraska 31, Michigan State 13 Up Next: Maryland It would be nice to have a stronger top win than Michigan State, but it was on the road – it beat the Spartans by more than Notre Dame did. Somewhat quietly, the Huskers have four double-digit blowout wins to start the season, and there will probably be a fifth next week against Maryland before hosting Indiana.

Record: (4-0) Last Week Rank: 26 Week 4: Virginia Tech 21, Boston College 14 Up Next: Pitt This falls into the "prove it, already" category, but we liked James Franklin's team all offseason, and it's getting the job done in workmanlike fashion so far. Now it has to beat an unbeaten Pitt team.

Record: (3-1) Last Week Rank: 19 Week 4: Iowa 20, Michigan 19 Up Next: at Minnesota The defense is so good that this bunch can hang with just about anyone, and the offense is so blah that we realize this is way too high. Don't blow off the Oklahoma win just because the Sooners got rocked by an amazing Georgia team; that was still a strong victory. But like Virginia Tech, there's a prove-it thing happening here. Go win the Little Brown Jug game at Minnesota next week, and the respect will follow.

Record: (4-0) Last Week Rank: 22 Week 4: Texas Tech 49, Sam Houston 14 Up Next: at Colorado We should probably be giving more respect to the win over Houston two weeks ago, but overall, this schedule is just so … meh. articles.title: Novak Djokovic has advice to give Iga Swiatek and promises they’ll talk more soon
articles.summary: Novak Djokovic may be 39 years of age with his powers waning, yet he remains one of tennis’ most integral and influential figures of all...
articles.body:
Novak Djokovic may be 39 years of age with his powers waning, yet he remains one of tennis' most integral and influential figures of all time.

Even today, as results may not be going his way, the Serbian is still a vital port of call for many of the sport's best players, with Iga Swiatek the latest to request his help.

Felix Auger-Aliassime, Joao Fonseca and Iva Jovic are three notable stars to have benefitted from his advice, whilst last year, Darren Cahill even attributed some of Sinner's success to advice Djokovic gave back in 2022.

The impact he has had on tennis goes far beyond the many, many trophies and accolades he has amassed.

Swiatek could be the latest set to enjoy an upturn in form because of his genius.

Iga Swiatek seeks advice from Novak Djokovic in Beijing

Djokovic's physio recently stated that he loves helping young players to improve their games, but Swiatek is hardly that.

She is no newcomer seeking a breakthrough moment; this is a six-time Grand Slam champion, who is just one Australian Open title away from completing the Career Grand Slam.

So, it arguably makes her request for his advice even more powerful, with one great champion bowing to another's superior experience and quality.

From the footage that emerged, it appeared that the Polish star was seeking counsel on her return position.

Novak Djokovic was heard noting: "As I said, I have a bit more wide like this, I try to have the feet open a little bit, I try to open a little bit more because… but it has evolved. When I was younger, I was standing a little more like this (bent over forward). Now, and then before, maybe five, six years ago, I was here (leaning back slightly). And now I'm here (middle ground stance). So, it's evolving."

He then added: "We'll talk more. My coach is already, I feel, here (gestures to the back of his neck). A lot of pressure."

Swiatek thanked him, and Djokovic insisted it was 'no problem'.

Djokovic, meanwhile, is set to make his first appearance since losing in the first round of the US Open late last month.

articles.title: Malaysia’s Ng, Subramaniam book LA28 Olympics berth with Asian Games gold
articles.summary: The top seeds defend their Asian Games squash titles, becoming the first players to qualify for the Los Angeles Games.
articles.body:
Malaysia’s Eain Yow Ng and Sivasangari Subramaniam have made history by becoming the first squash players to qualify for the 2028 Olympics after winning gold medals at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

The defending champions won the men’s and women’s singles finals on Sunday and earned a ticket to the 2028 Los Angeles Games, where squash will make its Olympic debut.

Squash is among a handful of sports at Aichi-Nagoya where a gold medal serves as automatic qualification for the next Olympics.

Both Ng and Subramaniam successfully defended their titles without dropping a single game in their campaigns. Their victories gave Malaysia its fifth and sixth gold medals.

World number 18 Ng thrashed India’s Abhay Singh 11-9, 11-5, 11-5 in 33 minutes at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena and became the first Malaysian to qualify for the Olympics.

World number five Subramaniam joined her compatriot soon after when she made quick work of the women’s final against India’s Anahat Singh.

She demolished Singh, ranked 17th in the world, 11-4, 11-4, 11-7 in just 23 minutes to clinch gold.

Earlier, Singh, the world junior champion, produced a stellar comeback in the semifinals from two sets down to overpower Japan’s Satomi Watanabe (9-11, 11-13, 12-10, 11-6, 11-3) on Saturday.

“I think it is the best win of my career,” Singh, 18, said after the match. “She’s number six in the world, and that’s the highest win I’ve ever had in my squash career.”

She made history even before Sunday’s match began when her semifinal victory made her the first Indian woman to reach the singles final at the Asian Games.

Earlier in the day, Pakistan picked up two more bronze medals at the games as third seed Noor Zaman toppled compatriot Ashab Irfan 3-0 in the bronze medal match. Watanabe took a 3-1 win over Hong Kong’s Sin Yuk Chan.

articles.title: Explaining New NHL Rule Changes for 2026-27 Season and Details on Stanley Cup Bracket
articles.summary: The new collective bargaining agreement the NHL and NHLPA ratified in July 2025 goes into effect on September 16, just ahead of the 2026–27 regular season. There are numerous changes affecting everything from on-ice play, off-ice behavior and financial/contract terms.
articles.body:
The new collective bargaining agreement the NHL and NHLPA ratified in July 2025 goes into effect on September 16, just ahead of the 2026–27 regular season. There are numerous changes affecting everything from on-ice play, off-ice behavior and financial/contract terms.

For instance, the CBA formally confirms NHL player participation in international events like the Winter Olympics following their return to the Milan Cortina 2026 games. It also eliminates the league-wide dress code, which will make for interesting game-day arrivals.

Other rules, including regular season expansion and changes to the salary cap and contract lengths, won't be as obvious on the ice but will greatly impact how teams retain talent.

Let's break down the biggest rule changes ahead of the 2026–27 NHL season.

The biggest change to the 2026–27 regular season will be in the number of games played. Every team will play 84 games, up from 82, for the first time since 1993–94.

Every team will play two additional games against divisional opponents, making it an even four games against every team in its division, two home and two away. This makes the divisional schedule much more uniform.

To offset the two extra in-season games, however, the new CBA reduces the number of preseason games to four max, with veterans who have 100+ career NHL games capped at playing in just two.

New Players Required to Wear Neck Protection

Beginning in 2026–27, any player with zero previous NHL games must wear cut-resistant neck protection, including goaltenders.

This rule is not retroactive, so if a player saw time in even one game before 2026– 27, neck protection remains optional.

The rule also applies during pregame warm-ups.

Sadly, in 2026–27 we must bid adieu to one of the greatest traditions in sports: random emergency backup goalies. Local Zamboni drivers and accountants can no longer suddenly get the call to appear in net, rush to the arena and enjoy a night of playing the game at the highest level.

Moving forward, teams must now designate a full-time, dedicated EBUG who travels with the team and participates in practices. This player must never have played an NHL game under a Standard Player Contract, must have played in fewer than 80 professional games at any level and cannot have played professional hockey in the past three seasons.

If activated during an emergency, the EBUG will sign either an amateur tryout or professional tryout contract, which allows them to sit on the bench without counting against the team's active roster limits.

The one positive of this new rule is that the designated EBUG can participate in practices and morning skates, which could mean more rest for regular goalies.

1 Prospect Every Team Can Get Hyped About 🤩

Teams must dress lineups that comply with the salary cap during the Stanley Cup Playoffs, closing the loophole that previously allowed teams to stash high-salary players on long-term injured reserve during the regular season and use that freed-up space to play an over-the-cap roster in the playoffs.

Maximum contract lengths are reduced to seven years for staying with a current team or six years for unrestricted free agents.

Singing bonuses are capped at 60% of total contract value, which prevents teams from handing out contracts where over 90% of the money is paid upfront in bonuses. Teams are also completely prohibited from deferring salary or bonus money on new deals. For front-loaded contracts, the salary and bonus difference between adjacent years cannot exceed 20% of first-year compensation (down from 25%).

The maximum contract length has been reduced to seven years, and six years for unrestricted free agents.

articles.title: Wigan Warriors: Matt Peet hurt by Super League play-off exit but 'proud' of side
articles.summary: Matt Peet says Wakefield were "far too good" for his Wigan side in Saturday's Super League play-off semi-final, with defeat ending their treble hopes.
articles.body:
Matt Peet conceded that Wakefield Trinity were "far too good" for his Wigan side in Saturday's Super League play-off semi-final - but he remains "proud" of the Warriors' team and their achievements this season.

Wigan were aiming to win a second domestic treble in three years, having already lifted the Challenge Cup and League Leaders' Shield, and went into the semi-final on a run of 16 successive victories.

But Wakefield's sensational 33-6 win ended their hopes of a third trophy in 2026 and sent Trinity through to their first-ever Grand Final.

"I'm always proud of the group," Wigan head coach Peet told BBC Radio Manchester after the loss.

"We'll be disappointed with the way it's finished and the time to reflect will be in a few weeks, but I'm proud of the group.

'Pipe dream' to reality? Wakefield reach Grand Final

Wakefield shock Wigan to reach first Grand Final

Hosts Wigan took the lead in the first half with Brad O'Neill's converted try, but Wakefield responded with 33 unanswered points either side of the interval.

"The night 100% belongs to Wakefield," added Peet. "Any time the season finishes, it's sad, but in that manner... we were off but Wakefield played excellent, which made us look that way.

"We were well beaten in every facet of the game and credit goes to Wakefield. We were prepared for a tough game but they were far too good for us."

Wakefield will play Warrington Wolves in the Grand Final at Old Trafford on Saturday, 3 October (18:00 BST).

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Tejaswin Shankar capped a demanding two days of competition with a victory in the final event, the 1500m, to secure the decathlon bronze at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya on Sunday.The Indian finished with 7,934 points after clocking 4:33.09 in the 1500m, winning the race ahead of Japan’s Yuma Maruyama. He seized it with a winning run, but Maruyama’s points advantage from the earlier events was enough to secure the Japanese athlete the title.The bronze added to India’s athletics medal haul, which had grown earlier on Sunday through Harita Bhadra’s third-place finish in the women’s 200m and Ancy Sojan’s silver in the women’s long jump.Ancy misses gold by two centimetresAncy came close to giving India its first athletics gold of the Games, but China’s Yingying Huang produced a decisive final-round jump to take the women’s long jump title. The No. 20 Oregon defeated No. 12 USC 41-27 at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on Saturday night, extending its winning streak over the Trojans to five games. The victory also gave Dan Lanning his third straight win against USC.

As he wrapped up his postgame press conference, he was asked about Oregon's growing influence in the West Coast recruiting battle. His response quickly turned into a shot at USC, with pop star Chris Brown caught in the crossfire.

articles.title: Film Review: Miami Hurricanes 52 – Central Michigan Chippewas 3
articles.summary: The Miami Hurricanes dominated the CMU Chips 52-3 at Hard Rock as a tune-up before Clemson in Death Valley.
articles.body:
The Miami Hurricanes ( 4-0 ) suffocated the Central Michigan Chippewas ( 2-2 ) 52-3 in Miami 's final cupcake game of the 2026 season. The Canyonero Keys to Victory main theme vs. CMU was to just play bully ball and smother the Chips. Miami played a balanced game with 34 passes and 34 runshing attempts.

The three keys to victory for Miami were:

1- Flores is the focus. QB Angel Flores was held to eight yards on three rushing attempts while CMU played three different QB's vs. the 'Canes. He was ineffective vs. Miami and that's what the Hurricanes had to do in order to hold CMU without a TD.

2- Clean up the OL play. Miami allowed two sacks and five TFL's but rushed for over 200 yards on 5.9 yards per carry including sack yardage. Ben Congdon came in at left guard and looked battle ready.

3- Get other WR's involved. Cooper Barkate and Daylyn Upshaw both scored, while Dre Jacobs got involved. But Malachi Toney is fine, folks. He only averaged 20 yards per catch with a TD reception.

Miami finished 7-of-10 on money downs as an offense, and allowed CMU to convert 6-of-14 tries while on defense. 70% is awesome, but allowing CMU anywhere near 50% is 'meh.'

The Hurricanes won the turnover battle with three takeaways vs. CMU. The 'Canes picked off and forced a fumble on QB Jadyn Glasser .

Miami lost the penalty yardage game after being flagged 13 times for 107 yards. CMU was flagged only six time for 36 yards.

Somourian Wingo looks like a viable KR/PR candidate with 22 yards per KR and a 42 yard PR. Anything to get Toney off of punt return unless Miami desperately needs a huge play. Jake Weinberg went 1-for-1 on FG's and 6-for-6 on PAT's.

Darian Mensah was on fire averaging 12.5 yards per pass attempt with three touchdowns and again, no interceptions. Mensah also had a rushing touchdown and looked healthy moving around on scrambles.

Mensah and Luke Nickel were able to connect with 12 different receivers with seven hitting double-digit yards per catch marks. Toney, Barkate, and Upshaw caught the TD passes from Mensah.

On the ground, Mark Fletcher Jr. sat out for precautionary reasons vs. CMU. A RB by committee approach was used and Girard Pringle and Javion Mallory battled for "RB2" with Marty Brown out. Pringle and Mallory averaged 5.4 and 6.0 yards per carry, respectively; and Mallory found the end zone .

Chris Wheatley-Humphrey looked like the next best option after those two, with Jordan Lyle struggling through 2.7 yards per carry. CWH averaged 9.5 yards per carry and scored one TD.

Above – Space creates time. Mensah decides to half roll but his RB thinks it's full roll. That allows a free runner. Mallory tries to block back on the pass rusher but Mensah decides to finish the rollout too late. It's a bad sack for Miami as Mensah gets whacked, but it's on Mensah.

Above- Max Buchanan does NOT in fact makes this block. And that player makes the stop. Miami needs to work on blocking in space with Okunlola, McCoy and Buchanan.

Above – Lofton with his head on the inside like it should be on a kick out block. Ben Congdon pulling and wrapping up to the 2nd level. Ben Congdon had a great game. It's still just the G6 but it's an improvement.

Above – Dawson called Mesh over and over again and it worked. Here it's the out route option with mesh inside. Upshaw runs such a solid out that the DB is looking entirely the wrong way.

Above – Congdon pulled, wrapped, and blocked the MDM. Miami has struggled in just picking up the first hat that shows vs. the 'perfect' hat that shows. Wabi sabi, y'all.

Above – Another ex. of Lofton pulling and getting his head on the right side, even if I want a little more shoulder there for a cut off. Condgdon dominating the combo and taking it over while Okunlola works to the LB. Look at that friggin bubble there.

Above – Chest and eyes back to the ball. No hip turn or basket here. The right way to ensure the catch.

Above – Lofton doing a fantastic job out in space blocking without holding. Congdon comes flying in to help once the RB works past the blocks from 9 and Barkate.

Above – Strong hands with eyes, hips, chest back to the ball. The best WR in CFB.

Above – This one isn't on Lyle. Okunlola completely misses his block and Lyle should have the edge but doesn't because of it which causes Lofton's guy to come free, too.

Above – Why Mesh in the red zone? It draws four defenders down leaving Barkate 1-on-1 on the post. TD Miami.

The 'Canes defense faced three Chips QB's and held the trio to 5.3 yards per pass attempt with one INT. The CMU passers found 11 different receivers, but only two averaged double-digit yards per catch marks.

The CMU rushing attack is their strength but Miami's defense smothered them most of the night. CMU averaged 0.8, yes , 0.8 yards per carry including four sacks and eight TFL's.

Marquis Lightfoot dominated for Miami once again. The elite edge rusher logged two sacks and 2.5 TFL's Omar Thornton picked up one sack and two TFL's from his flex-DB position. Justin Scott and Armondo Blount both picked up one TFL.

Above – The first three clips are all from the same play. It's power read. The read got cloudly for CMU with the overhang (Thornton here) also outside. Now the Q is taken by the DE and the RB is taken by the overhang. So what gives?

Above – Poyser has this tendency to over run the play and throw himself at the ball carrier. Here his head is across vs. behind the play, his eyes are down, and he leaves his feet.

Above – Tacklers have to learn to come to balance and shoot eyes to thighs with their head behind the play while grabbing the back of the ball carrier's thighs.

Above – Angles. This is a practiced art and Miami needs to work on their angles in space and the open field.

Above – If you're running under and getting beat by CMU, just wait for Clemson, Pitt, ND, etc.

Above – Here's the Justin Scott dominance we've been waiting for. He just grabs his guy and rides him into the TFL. Very Rueben Bain Jr. 'esque.

Above – Another look at power read with the DE and overhang in the backfield. The Q pulls and runs into Lightfoot of all people. I'd try to avoid that fella if I was a QB.

Above – Poyser is going to catch a lot of flack for winding up on the ground this much. He was so lost in his coverage that when he turned to find the ball he fell over.

Above – Another hole in coverage. Three defenders near it but no one truly covering.

The cupcake games are done. Expect more Wake Forest type games than CMU or Stanford . Miami won't get a Stanford again until Thanksgiving weekend vs. Boston College . Up next: Clemson, primetime, Death Valley. We'll get to the Clemson Tigers on Thursday's Film Forecast. For now, enjoy the win and seeing guys like Malachi Toney and Darian Mensah walking off healthy.

articles.title: How Gabe Jacas' brother turned a long shot into a Patriots pass rusher
articles.summary: As a chubby offensive lineman at 15, Gabe Jacas never pictured his football career lasting beyond high school. Everything changed when his brother, Khaliq, c...
articles.body:
The Patriots edge rusher recognized play action when Aaron Rodgers faked a handoff, pivoted quickly and came screaming upfield. Jacas arrived faster than Rodgers expected, belting the the 42-year-old to the turf and forcing an incompletion.

On his second defensive snap in Foxborough, the rookie had put a future Hall of Famer on the ground. Jacas then helped Rodgers up, and the two exchanged helmet taps. In the crowd, Khaliq Jacas smiled.

"It's exciting to see for sure, but it's not a surprise on my end," said Khaliq, Gabe's older brother. "(It's not) like, 'Oh my God, I can't believe he's doing this.' I knew he was gonna do it."

But not long ago, Khaliq was the only one who envisioned his younger brother as an NFL player — including Gabe himself.

As a chubby offensive lineman at 15 on Florida's Treasure Coast, Gabe never pictured his football career lasting beyond high school. Everything changed when Khaliq came home from college after Gabe's sophomore year. He saw more in his little brother. He saw greatness that just needed to be cultivated.

"Him having that vision, he brought that out of me," Gabe said. "He demanded that out of me because he saw it before I did. ...He didn't just let me be a waste."

Khaliq became a father figure, a coach and his best friend.

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers (8) is sacked by New England Patriots linebacker Gabe Jacas (50) during the first half of an NFL football game in Foxborough, Mass., Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Greg M. Cooper)AP Photo/Greg M. Cooper

When Khaliq returned home after graduating from Florida International University in 2020, something about Gabe had changed.

His kid brother's baby fat was beginning to melt off, replaced by lean muscle. He stood taller. Looking him in the eye, Khaliq saw a young man brimming with potential.

Khaliq was the eldest of four children, seven years older than Gabe. First-generation Americans with Jamaican roots, they were raised by their mother, Paula Henry, who worked as a registered nurse. Their father wasn't a consistent presence in their lives.

Khaliq had NFL dreams of his own that didn't come to fruition.

He began his collegiate career at ASA College, a JUCO in Hialeah, Florida. Then he made the leap to FIU for three seasons, where he was a 6-foot-2, 230-pound edge rusher and struggled to crack the lineup. After finishing school and heading back to Port St. Lucie, he'd come to grips with the fact that professional football wasn't going to happen for him.

Though he wasn't able to realize his own childhood dream, Khaliq had the blueprint now: A firsthand knowledge of how Division I football programs operate. He decided to pour everything he'd discovered into Gabe's future.

"I had aspirations, but with me, I was always a step behind. I never had the right guidance," Khaliq said. "So everything I learned, the do's and the don'ts, I made sure that Gabe was put in the best position possible."

He gave his brother a crash course in things he'd learned at FIU. He showed Gabe how to watch film and taught him how valuable proper nutrition would be. Khaliq told Gabe that natural ability might be enough to excel in high school, but if he wanted to be truly great, he needed to do more.

Khaliq also had a suggestion: Maybe it was time to flip from offensive line to the defensive side of the ball. Gabe was beginning to look like a dangerous edge rusher. Khaliq taught him pass rush moves and how to bend.

After a summer of training, it was time to take things up a notch.

Khaliq and Gabe Jacas at the University of Illinois (Courtesy: Khaliq Jacas)Khaliq Jacas

When Khaliq vowed to be there for Gabe, it meant he was always going to be there.

Khaliq is now a real estate agent, but he put that career on hold after college. Fort Pierce Central athletic director Pete Crespo is always looking for talented young coaches who can relate to players, so when Khaliq said he wanted to help at the high school, he was an easy hire.

Khaliq was brought on as an assistant football and wrestling coach — Gabe's two sports — and taught physical education classes as well. Whenever his brother needed something, he wasn't far. However, that didn't mean special treatment at practice.

"Man, I ain't gonna lie. On the field, you couldn't even tell it was my brother," Gabe said.

Khaliq was in charge of the defensive line and coached Gabe harder than anyone. His brother was never going to take plays off. He was going to run to every ball, no matter where it was on the field. He was always going to put extra work in.

Gabe relished the tough coaching. These things were forged into his DNA and still show up on film in Foxborough.

After practice, they'd grab dinner and then head to a gym nearby, spending more time working out and sharpening pass rush moves.

"He respected his brother," Crespo said. "He did what his brother told him to do and he trusts his brother. You know how sometimes brothers fight? That wasn't the case here. They never fought."

Well, almost never. There was one exception: When they stepped onto the wrestling mat during the winter season. Those matches were epic.

Though he was growing into a standout football player, Gabe might've been even more dominant as a wrestler.

As a junior, he won a 3A State Championship at 220 pounds. In his final season, he jumped up a weight class and wrestled as a heavyweight. There was one issue. Nobody else on the roster could challenge Gabe in practice.

Seven years older and fully grown, Khaliq put on wrestling gear and pushed his brother to the limit. It's what Gabe needed to be great. And once again, he didn't take it easy on him.

"Khaliq was willing to do whatever it took to get his brother to be an elite athlete," wrestling coach Pat Seidel said. "These guys were fighting over who gets the steak. It was an absolute brawl."

After that, most high school wrestlers didn't stand a chance as Gabe dominated, en route to a 45-2 season and a second 3A State Championship, this time in Florida's heaviest weight class. After Gabe pinned his final opponent of the year to win another ring, the Jacas brothers embraced.

"On the mat, it's kill or be killed," Seidel said. "Off the mat, it's a brotherhood that I envy myself. I have a brother. It's nothing like what I watched between those two. They're great. They're just best friends. Khaliq is really just there for him in any capacity."

Gabe and Khaliq Jacas on the field together after an Illinois game (Courtesy photo: Khaliq Jacas)Khaliq Jacas

When college football coaches started reaching out, Gabe was in a much better spot than Khaliq had been. While Khaliq was always a step behind, he had helped give his brother a leg up.

"I just feel like I was ahead of a lot of people," Gabe said.

When college coaches began coming to Fort Pierce Central to see Gabe, his advisor was already by his side. The first coach from Illinois to recruit Gabe was Aaron Henry, a former NFL safety. He met Khaliq the day he arrived in Port St. Lucie because he was working at the high school.

"That's Gabe's right hand," Henry said. "Everything kind of went through Khaliq and his mom. Khaliq was a great sounding board for him."

Gabe received offers from numerous Division I schools, Mississippi State, Tennessee , South Florida and Khaliq's school, FIU among them, but ultimately chose Illinois. He thrived as a four-year starter for the Illini and led the Big Ten with 11 regular-season sacks as a senior.

In the spring, he was widely expected to be a Day 2 draft pick and held a party that Friday night. Halfway through the second round, his phone lit up. Though the Chargers were set to pick at No. 55, it was Patriots executive Eliot Wolf on the other end of the line. New England traded up into that spot to ensure Jacas was going to be a Patriot.

As NFL commissioner Roger Goodell announced the pick on national television moments later, Jacas already had a navy blue Patriots hat on. The Jacas draft party erupted and Khaliq wrapped his arms around his little brother.

That moment gives Jacas goosebumps when he reflects on it.

Even five months later, while Khaliq was back in Florida, Jacas knew he wouldn't be standing in the Patriots locker room without his brother. He didn't refer to making the NFL as his accomplishment alone. It belonged to both of them.

"Everything we worked so hard for, our hopes and dreams, it came to life," Jacas said. "It's a testament of me, but it's also a testament of him. All this stuff he poured into me, we made it possible. We made it happen. It wasn't just a me thing... It just felt like everything we worked so hard for, it was worth it. The long nights, the early mornings, it was worth it. Now I will never, never stop doing that."

That relentlessness has proven valuable early in his tenure in Foxborough.

A knee injury and contract negotiation kept him sidelined for much of the spring, but when Jacas got on the field at training camp, his new coaches were bullish.

"I will tell you this, he looks like an outside linebacker," Mike Vrabel said. "I saw him in the uniform and said, 'Well, this is what they're supposed to look like.'"

Jacas recorded a sack in the season opener at Seattle and lived in the Steelers backfield last Sunday. In addition to knocking Rodgers to the turf, he intercepted the future Hall of Famer, too.

"Hey, great (expletive) job, man," a smiling Rodgers told Jacas on the field after the Patriots' 20-3 win.

When outside linebackers coach Mike Smith looks at Gabe now, he sees a confident 6-foot-4, 261-pound wrecking ball.

"You got a kid that's big like him, that's athletic like him, that's meaner than a wet mule, and he loves football," Smith said. "I'm not gonna say he's gonna be Jason Taylor or L.T. (Lawrence Taylor) or any of that stuff, but it's gonna be very hard for him to fail."

But Jacas might have failed if not for Khaliq's guidance.

He could have breezed through high school and hung up his cleats like he once thought he would. Instead, he got the blueprint for success from Khaliq and that's made all the difference.

"He stepped up in that (father figure) role and he embraced it," Jacas said. "He didn't shy away from it. He didn't bat an eye. He stepped up in that role. Being the older brother, he filled that role of, 'OK, Dad's not really around, but I'm a bigger brother and I'll help you any way I can.' It wasn't always perfect, but it was more than enough."

articles.title: Sophia Moss brings international experience to FSU volleyball
articles.summary: Outside hitter Sofia Moss brings international experience to Seminoles volleyball, following in her mother's footsteps as a professional player.
articles.body:
Florida State freshman outside hitter Sophia Moss is paving the way for international athletes on the Seminole women's volleyball team. A native of Tortoli, Italy, she is the only Italian-born player in program history.

Moss is transforming that landmark journey into on-the-court production, most recently tying her career high with a 14-kill performance against the University of North Alabama on Sept. 14. With every kill and dig, she continues to carve out her legacy at FSU, a path that first began with her mom in Italy.

"[My mom] was a professional volleyball player, [and] she was my first coach," Moss said in an interview with the FSView. "She still coaches me today … sometimes it's four a.m., she watches my game, and we call later, and she tells me [advice]."

That mentorship from Moss' mother paid dividends, as Moss earned the opportunity to play professional volleyball in Italy at 15. She made her club volleyball debut with Selezione Regionale Sardegna U16 in 2021. Over the next five years, she played for Pan Alfieri Cagliari, Volleyró Casal de Pazzi, and Club Italia prior to joining the 'Noles.

That level of competition uniquely prepared Moss for Division I volleyball with the Garnet and Gold.

"I used to play against teams that had volleyball players that were older than me … they [were] 30 years old," Moss said. "I also always played with players that were older than me, so I think that was great for me and for my development."

Moss' volleyball development also stems from a multi-sport background, which she credits her father for.

"I used to play tennis, and my dad was my coach," Moss said. "I think a lot of things in tennis help me in volleyball … coordination is very important in tennis, [which] helped me so much [in volleyball] ... I also think playing tennis helped me to be more fast."

That combination of early competition and multi-sport training prepared Moss mentally and physically for her next step: a 5,906-mile move to Tallahassee.

"[Head coach] Lindsay [Allman] called me to show me the project of this year, [and] for me it was very good," Moss said. "The coach, the staff [and] all [of] my teammates; they support me … it's very different from home, but I really like it."

The support from her teammates and coaches continues to translate to production on the volleyball court. Moss has tallied double-digit kills in four games and double-digit digs in three games this season.

Still, Moss and the women's volleyball team have faced early challenges. Florida International University defeated Florida State in three sets Sept. 13, marking the first time the Seminoles were swept this season.

Despite the early adversity, Moss is still looking to prove herself.

"My goal is to grow … as a player," Moss said. "I want to be a better player for my team … and to win the most we can. I think we can be better than [we are] now, but it's a new team, and it's normal that in the start there are some difficulties, but I think we can [have] a great season if we work hard. We want to win, and if we work, we will win."

For Moss, it is not just about winning games, it is about getting to represent Italy at the highest level in American collegiate athletics. Moss's opportunity to receive that honor only came because of change, something she believes international athletes should continue to embrace.

"I think a lot of people are afraid of change, and they don't know that they [will] lose a big opportunity," Moss said. "I know it's hard to be far from home [and] from your friends, but I think sometimes … the right choice is to get out of your comfort zone. I think we international [student athletes] must not be afraid of that change because change is beautiful."

Hunter Milligan is a Senior Staff Writer for the FSView & Florida Flambeau, the student-run, independent online news service for the FSU and Tallahassee communities. Email our staff at contact@fsview.com .
